title: The Skipped-Lunch Sprint
briefing: Ravi, 14, skipped lunch for a club meeting and has track practice at 4 p.m. The warm-up jog feels fine. In the 200 m sprints he is gasping, his legs turn to jelly, his hands shake, and he stops after two of four. His teammate Ji-woo, who ate lunch, gasps just as hard — and finishes all four.
question: What made Ravi stop when Ji-woo didn't?

clues.title: Breakfast at 7, nothing since
clues.text: Breakfast was at 7 a.m. and he skipped lunch. By practice it's been nine hours without food.
clues.shows: nine hours with nothing to refill his fuel

clues.title: Shaky hands, fuzzy head
clues.text: Between sprints his hands tremble and he has trouble remembering how many reps are left.
clues.shows: brain and muscles short of fuel

clues.title: Gasping in the sprints — like everyone
clues.text: At sprint pace Ravi takes about 45 breaths a minute with his heart pounding. Ji-woo is breathing just as hard.
clues.shows: muscles demanding lots of oxygen at sprint pace, the same for anyone

clues.title: Fine on the warm-up jog
clues.text: The easy jog felt normal. The trouble only started when the pace went up to sprinting.
clues.shows: the problem appearing only when the effort is high

hypotheses.text: Both: sprinting makes muscles burn fuel and oxygen very fast (that's the hard breathing everyone has), and after nine hours without food Ravi had less fuel to burn — so his muscles ran short at sprint pace even though jogging was fine.
He's low on fuel because he skipped lunch.
hypotheses.flaw: If it were only fuel, the easy warm-up jog would have been a struggle too.

hypotheses.text: Sprinting is just very hard — everyone breathes like that.
hypotheses.flaw: Ji-woo sprinted just as hard and finished; hard work alone doesn't explain shaky hands or why Ravi had to stop.

hypotheses.text: His running shoes are worn out.
hypotheses.flaw: Worn shoes don't make your hands shake or your head fuzzy.

prediction.prompt: Ravi hasn't eaten for nine hours. As he runs harder — from resting to sprinting — what happens to the fuel his muscles have available?

second.question: And what happens to his breathing rate?

concepts.label: fuel from food
concepts.hint: What do muscles burn to work?

concepts.label: a long gap since eating
concepts.hint: Why was Ravi's supply low today?

concepts.label: breathing delivers oxygen
concepts.hint: Why was everyone gasping in the sprints?

concepts.label: fuel burns faster than it's replaced
concepts.hint: What happens to fuel at sprint pace?

transfer.context: Maya plays three soccer games in a tournament. Game one at 9 a.m. goes great, but in the third game at 3 p.m. — with only a granola bar since breakfast — her legs feel heavy and she can't keep up in the sprints, though she can still jog fine.
options: Hard sprints burn muscle fuel fast, and with little food since breakfast her muscles ran short at high effort.
transfer.retryHint: She's fine jogging but not sprinting, many hours after a real meal — which of Ravi's clues was that?
transfer.explanation: Maya's third game asked her muscles for fuel at sprint pace after hours with little to eat. Jogging uses fuel slowly enough to get by; sprinting burns it faster than her low supply could keep up with — the same pairing that stopped Ravi.

takeaway: Effort and fuel are a pair. Sprinting makes everyone breathe hard because muscles burn fuel and oxygen fast; whether you can keep going depends on how much fuel is left. Lungs deliver the oxygen; food supplies the fuel.
